problems.title: Covering an HD image
problems.statement: A 1920 × 1080 image, blocks of 16 × 16 threads, one thread per pixel.
problems.solution: (a) $1920/16 = 120$. (b) $\lceil 1080/16 \rceil = 68$. (c) The grid covers $1920 \times 1088$ pixels: 8 extra rows of 1,920 threads, $15{,}360$ threads that the guard must stop.

problems.title: Row-major addressing
problems.statement: An RGB image of width 640 is stored row-major with 3 bytes per pixel.

parts.prompt: Byte index of the blue channel (c = 2) of pixel (x, y) = (37, 12)?
Which pixel comes right after (639, 0) in memory? Give its y.

hints: Pixel index $y W + x$, times 3, plus the channel.
problems.solution: (a) $(12 \times 640 + 37) \times 3 + 2 = 7717 \times 3 + 2 = 23,153$. (b) After the last pixel of row 0 comes pixel (0, 1): rows are laid end to end, so y = 1.

problems.title: Who am I?
problems.statement: A 2-D launch with blockDim = (16, 8). A thread has blockIdx = (3, 2) and threadIdx = (5, 7). The image is 200 pixels wide.

parts.prompt: The linear (row-major) index of its pixel?

problems.title: A square image, a wide block
problems.solution: (a) $32 \times 125 = 4{,}000$ blocks. (b) $4000 \times 256 = 1{,}024{,}000$ threads. (c) $97.66\%$: only the x-direction overhangs, by 24 columns (1,024 − 1,000).

problems.title: A grid-stride loop, exactly
problems.statement: A grid-stride loop over $n = 10{,}000$ elements runs with 20 blocks of 64 threads.

parts.prompt: How many threads run that many?
How many warps diverge on the final loop test?

hints: Thread $t$ handles $t, t + S, t + 2S, \ldots$ while below $n$.
Which warp contains the first thread that runs one iteration fewer?
problems.solution: (a) $S = 1280$. (b, c) $10000 = 7 \times 1280 + 1040$, so threads $0$–$1039$ run 8 iterations and the rest 7. (d) Thread 1040 is lane 16 of global warp 32: that warp's lanes 0–15 continue and 16–31 stop, so it diverges. Every other warp is uniform. Only one warp out of 40 pays, and only once.

problems.title: Three billion elements
problems.statement: A 1-D kernel over $3 \times 10^9$ elements uses 256 threads per block and computes int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x; with a 32-bit signed int.

parts.prompt: The first index that doesn't fit in a 32-bit signed int?

options: Indices past that point wrap to negative values and access the wrong memory
CUDA promotes the arithmetic to 64-bit automatically
Nothing: the grid limit prevents it

problems.solution: (a) $\lceil 3\times10^9/256 \rceil = 11,718,750$ blocks, well inside the x limit, so the launch succeeds. (b) $2^{31}$. (c) The product is computed in 32 bits and wraps (formally undefined behaviour for signed ints), so threads past 2.1 billion index garbage. Compute the index in 64 bits: size_t i = size_t(blockIdx.x) * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x.

problems.title: A 3-D volume
problems.statement: A 256 × 256 × 128 volume (x × y × z), stored with x fastest, then y, then z. Blocks are 8 × 8 × 8.

parts.prompt: Linear index of voxel (x, y, z) = (10, 20, 30)?

problems.title: A very tall image

parts.prompt: gridDim.y needed for a direct 2-D launch?
Can that launch run in CUDA?

options: Swap the roles: map rows to blockIdx.x
Use a grid-stride loop over y with a smaller grid
Use 1024 × 1 blocks with the same grid
Launch a 1-D grid over all pixels and recover (x, y) by division

hints: Limits: x up to $2^{31}-1$, y and z up to 65,535.
problems.solution: (a) $2{,}000{,}000/16 = 125{,}000 > 65{,}535$, so (b) the launch fails. (c) Moving the large dimension to x, looping over y with a grid-stride loop, or a flat 1-D launch all work. Changing the block shape doesn't help: 1024 × 1 blocks need 2,000,000 blocks in y.

problems.title: When the grid-stride loop pays
problems.statement: A kernel spends 50 instructions per thread on setup (index arithmetic, loading parameters, computing a table pointer) and 10 per element. A grid-stride loop adds 2 instructions of loop overhead per element. $n = 2^{24}$.

parts.prompt: Total instructions with one thread per element?
Total with a grid-stride loop over 32,768 threads (the GW-1 full)?

hints: One thread per element pays setup $n$ times.
Grid-stride pays it 32,768 times, and 12 per element.
problems.solution: (a) $2^{24} \times 60 = 1,006,632,960$. (b) $32768 \times 50 + 2^{24} \times 12 = 202,964,992$. (c) 4.96×. The heavier the per-thread setup relative to the per-element work, the more a machine-sized grid wins, and it also makes the launch size independent of $n$.

problems.title: 4K
problems.solution: $3840/32 = 120$ and $2160/8 = 270$: 32,400 blocks, no overhang. Standard video sizes are friendly to power-of-two blocks in x, less so in y (1080 isn't a multiple of 16).
